name: Sri Maha Bodhi
openHours: Worship from about 6:00–21:00. The ticket counter follows archaeological hours, about 7:00–17:30.
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 30 (Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay much less, and worshippers are often admitted free.
description: This sacred fig tree in the Mahamewuna gardens grew from a cutting of the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. Sanghamitta Theri brought the sapling in the 3rd century BCE, and it is the oldest historically recorded tree planted by people. It stands at the heart of the Sacred City of Anuradhapura, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
etiquette: Remove shoes and hats, cover shoulders and knees, and do not turn your back on the tree. Keep voices low and do not pick leaves.

name: Ruwanwelisaya
openHours: About 6:00–21:00 for worship. Ticket sales follow archaeological hours, about 7:00–17:30.
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 30 (Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay much less or enter free to worship.
description: King Dutugemunu built this great white stupa in the 2nd century BCE. It is one of the Solosmasthana, the sixteen most sacred Buddhist places in Sri Lanka, and it is still an active place of worship inside the UNESCO Sacred City of Anuradhapura.
etiquette: Remove shoes, dress modestly, and walk clockwise around the stupa. Lotus flowers are a traditional offering. Do not climb the dome.

name: Jetavanaramaya
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 30 (Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay a lower local rate.
description: King Mahasena raised this brick stupa in the 3rd century CE. It was one of the tallest structures of the ancient world and belonged to a great monastery that once housed thousands of monks. The stupa is part of the UNESCO Sacred City of Anuradhapura.
etiquette: Stay on the paths and do not climb the brickwork. A modest dress code still applies because this is a sacred monument.

name: Thuparamaya
openHours: About 6:00–18:00. Ticket sales follow archaeological hours, about 7:00–17:30.
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 30 (Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay much less or enter free to worship.
description: King Devanampiya Tissa built Thuparamaya in the 3rd century BCE after Arahat Mahinda introduced Buddhism. It is regarded as the oldest stupa in Sri Lanka and is said to enshrine a collarbone relic of the Buddha. The stone columns around it once carried a circular roof.
etiquette: Remove shoes, dress modestly, and walk around the stupa rather than across its platform edges. Do not lean on the ancient columns.

name: Isurumuniya Vihara
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 30 (Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay a lower local rate.
description: King Devanampiya Tissa founded this rock temple in the 3rd century BCE. Visitors come for the temple, the bathing pond, and the famous stone carving of a couple known as the Isurumuniya Lovers. It sits at the southern edge of the UNESCO Sacred City of Anuradhapura.
etiquette: Remove shoes inside the temple. Do not touch the carvings, and ask before photographing people who are worshipping.

name: Mihintale
openHours: About 6:00–18:00. Go early; the stairway is exposed and hot by late morning.
entryFee: A separate modest ticket is sold at the foot of the mountain. This is not the Anuradhapura sacred-city ticket. Sri Lankan visitors pay less.
description: Mihintale is where Arahat Mahinda met King Devanampiya Tissa in the 3rd century BCE, the meeting remembered as the start of Buddhism in Sri Lanka. A long stone stair leads to the Ambastala stupa and the meditation rock called Aradhana Gala. The site is a short drive east of Anuradhapura and is not inside the UNESCO city boundary.
etiquette: Dress modestly. Remove shoes at shrine terraces. Do not shout on the meditation rock, and carry water for the climb.

name: Sigiriya
openHours: About 7:00–17:30. Last entry is earlier than closing because the climb takes time.
entryFee: Foreign adults: USD 35 full ticket (Central Cultural Fund, October 2026). Half ticket about USD 20. Sri Lankan visitors pay a small local rate.
description: King Kashyapa built a palace on this rock in the 5th century, during the Anuradhapura period. The visit passes water gardens, the mirror wall with old graffiti, the remaining frescoes, and the lion staircase. UNESCO listed Ancient City of Sigiriya in 1982.
etiquette: Do not touch the frescoes or write on the mirror wall. The stairs are steep; turn back if the weather turns wet. Drones are not allowed.

name: Rangiri Dambulla Cave Temple
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 10. Sri Lankan visitors pay less. Shoes are left at the entrance.
description: Five caves in a rock above Dambulla hold Buddha images and murals. King Valagamba first used the caves in the 1st century BCE, and Kandyan kings later restored the paintings. UNESCO listed the Golden Temple of Dambulla in 1991.
etiquette: Cover shoulders and knees. Remove shoes and hats before the caves. Do not use flash, touch paintings, or pose with your back to the statues.

name: Gal Vihara
openHours: About 7:00–17:30, with the rest of Ancient Polonnaruwa.
entryFee: Foreign adults: USD 30 (Polonnaruwa ancient-city ticket, Central Cultural Fund, October 2026). One ticket covers the main ruins, including this site.
description: Four Buddha figures were cut from a single granite cliff in the 12th century under King Parakramabahu I. They show the Buddha seated, standing, and reclining. Gal Vihara is part of the UNESCO Ancient City of Polonnaruwa.
etiquette: Do not climb or touch the sculptures. Stay behind the rails, and dress modestly because people still venerate the images.

name: Polonnaruwa Vatadage
entryFee: Foreign adults: USD 30 (Polonnaruwa ancient-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay a lower local rate.
description: The vatadage is a round relic house built beside the Quadrangle in Polonnaruwa. Guards-stones, moonstones, and Buddha images remain around the central stupa. It is one of the finest stone buildings of the UNESCO Ancient City of Polonnaruwa.
etiquette: Do not walk on moonstones or sit on the carved stones. Keep to the marked paths.

name: Rankoth Vehera
entryFee: Foreign adults: USD 30 (Polonnaruwa ancient-city ticket). Sri Lankan visitors pay a lower local rate.
description: Rankoth Vehera is the largest stupa in Polonnaruwa. King Nissankamalla built it in the 12th century, copying the great stupas of Anuradhapura. It stands in the northern group of monuments inside the UNESCO city.
etiquette: Walk clockwise if you circumambulate the stupa. Do not climb the dome or leave plastic offerings.

name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
openHours: About 5:30–20:00. The shrine is busiest at the daily pujas in the early morning, late morning, and evening.
entryFee: Foreign adults from countries other than SAARC, Thailand, and Myanmar: LKR 3,000 (temple's own ticket). SAARC, Thailand, and Myanmar: LKR 2,500. Sri Lankan visitors are free. Buy tickets only from the temple machines.
description: Sri Dalada Maligawa houses a tooth relic of the Buddha and was the royal temple of the Kandyan kingdom. The present buildings took shape in the 17th and 18th centuries beside the lake. The temple is part of the UNESCO Sacred City of Kandy.
etiquette: Remove shoes and hats. Cover shoulders and knees. Do not photograph the relic chamber, and keep quiet during puja.

name: Galle Fort
openHours: The streets and ramparts are open through the day and evening. Museums keep shorter daytime hours.
entryFee: Free to walk the fort. The National Museum inside the fort is about USD 6 for foreign adults.
description: The Portuguese began a fort at Galle, and the Dutch rebuilt it in the 17th century as a walled town. Churches, Dutch houses, and the rampart clock remain inside a living neighbourhood. UNESCO listed the Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications in 1988.
etiquette: It is a home as well as a monument. Do not block doorways, fly drones from the walls, or climb unsafe rampart edges.

name: Jaffna Fort
entryFee: Grounds are often free to walk. A Central Cultural Fund ticket of about USD 5 may apply to the Jaffna site or its museum. Ask at the gate.
description: The Portuguese raised a fort on the Jaffna lagoon in the 17th century, and the Dutch expanded it into a five-sided stronghold. It was badly damaged during the civil war and has since been restored. The ramparts look across the lagoon toward the town.
etiquette: Keep to open ramparts and do not enter closed or unsafe rooms. Be respectful; the fort is a reminder of both colonial rule and the recent war.

name: Nallur Kandaswamy Kovil
openHours: About 5:00–12:00 and 16:00–19:00. The twenty-five-day festival is usually in August.
entryFee: Free. Donations are welcome.
description: This is the principal kovil of Jaffna, dedicated to Lord Murugan. An earlier temple stood here in the Jaffna kingdom; the Portuguese destroyed it, and the present temple was rebuilt from the 18th century. The gopuram and festival chariot processions are the best-known sights.
etiquette: Men are expected to remove their shirts before the inner courts. Everyone should leave shoes outside and avoid shorts or sleeveless clothes.

name: Koneswaram Temple
entryFee: Free. Donations are welcome.
description: Koneswaram stands on Swami Rock above the Indian Ocean. Tamil hymns praise the ancient shrine of Konesar. The Portuguese destroyed the cliff temple in 1622, and the present building was consecrated in the 20th century.
etiquette: Remove shoes, dress modestly, and follow the priests' directions near the sanctum. The cliff edge is unfenced in places, so keep back from the drop.

name: Jami Ul-Alfar Mosque
openHours: Visitors are welcome outside prayer times, often mid-morning and mid-afternoon. Avoid Friday midday prayers.
entryFee: Free.
description: The Red Mosque in Pettah was completed in 1909 for Colombo's Muslim trading community. Its red-and-white striped brickwork mixes Indo-Islamic design with the busy market streets around it. It is still a working mosque.
etiquette: Dress modestly. Women should bring a headscarf. Remove shoes, stay quiet, and do not walk in front of people who are praying.

name: Kechimalai Mosque
openHours: Visit between prayers, roughly 9:00–11:30 and 14:00–16:30. Avoid Friday midday prayers.
entryFee: Free.
description: Kechimalai Mosque at Beruwala sits on a headland above the fishing harbour. Tradition says Arab traders founded a mosque here around the 10th century, which would make it one of the oldest in Sri Lanka. The white building seen today is a later rebuilding of that old foundation.
etiquette: Dress modestly, remove shoes, and women should cover their hair. Ask before photographing worshippers or the interior.

name: Yapahuwa Rock Fortress
entryFee: A modest ticket is sold at the gate. Foreign visitors pay more than Sri Lankan visitors. Confirm the current price on site.
description: Yapahuwa was a short-lived capital in the 13th century, after Polonnaruwa fell and during the Dambadeniya period. The tooth relic was kept here for a time. A steep ornamental stair, with lions and dancers carved beside it, climbs the rock.
etiquette: Do not climb the carved stair rails. The upper rock is steep and slippery after rain.

name: Lankatilaka Viharaya
entryFee: Free, or a small donation at the temple office. There is no large Cultural Triangle ticket.
description: King Bhuvanekabahu IV built Lankatilaka in the 14th century on a rock at Hiyarapitiya, west of Kandy. It is a Gampola-era image house, with tall brick walls and later Kandyan paintings. The white temple is reached by a long flight of steps.
etiquette: Remove shoes and hats. Cover shoulders and knees. Do not touch the murals.

name: Embekke Devalaya
entryFee: Free, or a small donation. There is no large Cultural Triangle ticket.
description: Embekke is a 14th-century shrine of the Gampola kingdom, dedicated to Kataragama Deviyo, a guardian deity worshipped alongside Buddhism. Its wooden audience hall is famous for carved pillars of wrestlers, swans, and dancers. The drummers' hall still stands beside the shrine.
etiquette: Remove shoes. This is a living devalaya, so keep quiet during rituals and ask before taking close photographs of priests.

name: Buduruwagala
entryFee: Foreign adults: about USD 3 (Central Cultural Fund, October 2026). Sri Lankan visitors pay less.
description: Seven figures are carved into a rock face near Wellawaya. The central Buddha stands about 16 metres tall, with bodhisattva figures beside him, and the group is usually dated to the 9th or 10th century. Traces of the original plaster and paint can still be seen.
etiquette: Do not climb the rock or wet the carvings. Stay behind any barrier and leave offerings only in the places provided.

name: Tissamaharama Raja Maha Vihara
entryFee: Free for worship. A small local donation is customary.
description: This great stupa was the religious centre of the southern kingdom of Ruhuna. Kings of the 2nd and 3rd centuries BCE, including Kavantissa, are linked with its founding. The white dagoba and its tank sit in the town of Tissamaharama, near Yala.
etiquette: Remove shoes, dress modestly, and walk clockwise around the stupa. Do not fly kites or play music in the courtyard.

name: Star Fort
entryFee: Free to enter the fort.
description: The Dutch built this small star-shaped fort in 1763–1765, after a rebellion in Matara. Its points let cannons cover every approach from the Nilwala River side. A modest gateway with the Dutch VOC monogram still faces the street.
etiquette: The interior is small and sometimes used for local offices or a museum. Do not cross ropes or climb the outer walls.

name: Wolvendaal Church
openHours: Usually open in the daytime, about 8:00–16:00, except during services.
entryFee: Free.
description: Wolvendaal Church, also called the Dutch Reformed Church, was consecrated in 1757. It is the oldest Protestant church in Colombo still used for worship. Thick walls, Dutch tombstones, and canopied chairs survive in the nave.
etiquette: Sit quietly and do not walk around during a service. Ask the caretaker before photographing funerary stones or using flash.
